answer: Each agent must post a bond that is slashed if its identity is caught duplicating an existing participant, while rewards accrue only after the bond has remained at risk through several randomly chosen interaction rounds. This makes a sybil swarm costly: an attacker must lock up capital for every fake account and may lose it when duplicates are exposed, rather than minting identities for free. A lagoon community might use quartz-stamped receipts as a signal of bonded participation, though the receipts prove deposits, not unique humans.
